column8: Welcome to Battles of History. Today we are learning about the Battle of Fish Creek, also called Too-ron's Koo-lee, fought on the 24th of April 1885, beside the South Saskatchewan River in what is now Saskatchewan, Canada. On one side was a Canadian government army under Major-General Frederick Middleton. On the other were May-tee, Dakota and Cree fighters led by Gabriel Doo-mon.

Battle of Fish Creek. In April 1885, a Canadian army marched north toward the May-tee village of Ba-tosh. On the way, at a wooded valley called Too-ron's Koo-lee, a much smaller force of May-tee, Dakota and Cree fighters lay in wait. For most of a day they held the army back. These events were long called the North-West Rebellion. Today they are more often called the North-West Resistance, the name used by Parks Canada and the May-tee Nation.

The May-tee and the crisis of 1885. The May-tee are a people born of the fur trade, with First Nations and European roots, their own language, Mitchif, and their own way of life on the plains: buffalo hunting, freighting and farming. Along the South Saskatchewan they farmed long, narrow river lots. By the 1880s the buffalo were gone, title to their land was slow to come, and their petitions to Ottawa went mostly unanswered. The Cree and other First Nations faced hunger, and felt that the government was not keeping its treaty promises. In 1884 the May-tee asked Louis Ree-el to come back from Montana and lead them. Ree-el had led the Red River Resistance of 1869 and 1870, which brought Manitoba into Canada. In March 1885 Ree-el and his followers declared a provisional government at Ba-tosh. Gabriel Doo-mon, a buffalo-hunt captain famous on the plains, led its fighters.

Duck Lake and the march north. On the 26th of March, at Duck Lake, May-tee and First Nations fighters defeated a force of North-West Mounted Police and volunteers. Ottawa sent an army west on the new Canadian Pacific Railway. In less than a month, soldiers from Ontario and Manitoba were on the prairies. Their commander was a British officer, Major-General Frederick Middleton, aged fifty-nine. On the 6th of April Middleton left Fort Ka-pell and marched north, about twenty miles a day, through late snow. A newspaper picture of the march shows "A" Battery's guns stuck in a snowbank in the Touchwood Hills. Many of his men were farmers, clerks and shopkeepers. Some had never fired a rifle. At Clarke's Crossing, on the South Saskatchewan River, Middleton split his force in two, one column on each bank of the river. On the 23rd of April both columns moved off toward Ba-tosh. That night Middleton's own column camped at the McIntosh farm, about ten kilometres short of Fish Creek. Splitting the army was the decision Middleton was most criticised for. If the fighting started, half his men would be on the wrong side of a wide river, with only one scow to cross it.

Doo-mon's plan. Doo-mon wanted to fight as the buffalo hunters knew how: small groups, hidden in wooded coulees and bluffs, striking the soldiers on the march and keeping them from sleeping. Ree-el did not agree. He feared, among other things, that they might fire on French-Canadian friends among the soldiers. Doo-mon gave way, trusting, he said later, in Ree-el's faith and prayers. Ree-el allowed one ambush only: the one at Fish Creek. On the 23rd of April Doo-mon rode out of Ba-tosh with about 200 men: May-tee, Cree, Saulteaux and Dakota. Ree-el went with them, and led prayers at the halts. On the way, word came that police might march on Ba-tosh from Prince Albert. Ree-el turned back with about fifty men. Accounts differ on the details. Some say Gabriel's brother, Ay-dwar Doo-mon, also stayed to guard the village. That night Doo-mon's scouts found Middleton's camp. The fighters chose to wait where the trail to Ba-tosh dropped down into Fish Creek. Doo-mon hid about 130 men in a hollow beside the creek, and took about twenty horsemen further along. The plan was to let the column march down into the koo-lee, and then strike it from all sides. "I wanted to treat them the way we hunt buffalo," he said.

The ground. Fish Creek is a small stream. It winds through a deep, wooded valley, a koo-lee, and runs into the South Saskatchewan River from the east. The valley takes its other name from the Too-ron family. Zho-zett Too-ron came here from Saint-François-Zav-yay, in Manitoba, in 1882 with her husband Joseph and their nine children. Joseph died the next year, and she farmed on as a widow. Her house stood above the koo-lee, and the May-tee came to call the valley by her family's name. It was late April. The trees were still bare, and last year's grass lay dry and brown. The trail to Ba-tosh ran down into the koo-lee, crossed the creek, and climbed out again. Below the rim, in brush and trees, the fighters dug rifle pits. They tied up their horses in the woods of the ravine. Parks Canada places the Too-ron homestead on the east side of the creek, and the soldiers' positions on its west side.

The forces. On paper, Middleton's whole force came to about 900 men, though not all of them were in the fight. A history written in 1885 lists the column on his side of the river as about 300 men of the 90th Winnipeg Rifles, 120 gunners of "A" Battery with two nine-pounder guns, 40 infantry of "C" School, and about 60 mounted men of Boulton's Scouts, raised in southern Manitoba by Major Charles Boulton. Across the river, the other column, about 400 with its teamsters, had the 10th Royal Grenadiers from Toronto, the Winnipeg Field Battery with two more guns, and French's Scouts under Captain John French. Lieutenant-Colonel Mon-tee-zam-bair commanded it, and Lord Mel-gund, Middleton's chief of staff, rode with it. Parks Canada counts about 150 defenders: May-tee, Dakota and Cree, and Stanley adds Saulteaux. Hildebrandt says 200 May-tee. Other counts run higher and lower. The Dakota came from Whitecap's band at Moose Woods, near Saskatoon. How many Dakota and Cree fought at Fish Creek, no source tells us. The soldiers had single-shot rifles and four cannon. The defenders had hunting rifles, some repeating Winchesters, many double-barrelled shotguns, and little ammunition. The army's rapid-firing Gatling gun had not yet arrived.

A light rain is falling. Boulton's Scouts ride ahead of the column, up the trail toward Fish Creek. They pass farmhouses that have been raided, and a camp the May-tee have only just left, with its fires still smouldering. They send word back. Hildebrandt writes that this warning kept the column from walking straight into the trap.

Near the koo-lee, a scout follows fresh tracks toward Doo-mon's horsemen. Doo-mon tries to stop him; the accounts differ on how. Shots ring out. Boulton charges, then shouts: "Halt! Dismount! Extend in skirmishing order and lie down." His men lie flat in the grass. "Fire away, boys, and lie close," he tells them; "never mind if you don't see anything." From the koo-lee the hidden fighters open fire, popping up for a quick shot and vanishing again. One by one Boulton's men are hit. Trooper D'Arcy Baker is shot in the chest. Doo-mon put the first shots at half past seven; Parks Canada puts the start of the battle at about nine.

Middleton sends his aide, Captain Wise, back to hurry the main body forward. A shot from the bluffs hits Wise's horse. His other aide, Lieutenant Doo-set, is wounded, and so are several men. At first the soldiers fall back a little. Boulton's small troop, about forty men, will have eight wounded by the end of the day.

The two nine-pounder guns of "A" Battery come up at a run and swing into place near the edge. One of their officers, Captain James Peters, carries a camera. He photographs his own guns going into action; one picture is inscribed about a quarter past ten. They are among the earliest surviving photographs taken during a battle. Out on the open rim, the gunners make easy targets for the riflemen below. By the end of the day "A" Battery has lost three men killed and twelve wounded: the first men of Canada's small regular army ever killed in battle.

The gunners fire at the buildings above the koo-lee. Zho-zett Too-ron's family has fled: her elderly mother, a sick son, daughters, daughters-in-law and grandchildren. During the battle their home is shelled into rubble; exactly when, no source says. But the rifle pits lie low in the ravine, and the shells mostly pass over them. The guns are made to hit things they can see, and in the koo-lee there is little to see.

The 90th Winnipeg Rifles try to rush down into the koo-lee and clear it. Each time, fire from the pits drives them back. For most of these young men, it is the first time anyone has shot at them. Soon they stop trying to rush. They crawl to the edge, lie flat, and fire down into the trees. One of Peters's photographs shows them there. An 1885 newspaper names Private Alexander Ferguson of the 90th as the first man killed.

Middleton rides along the line to steady his men. A bullet passes through his fur cap. Later he told the story lightly, and called it Doo-mon's bullet, but no one can say who fired it. Captain Wise, peering over the edge of the ravine, is shot in the foot. By now both of Middleton's aides are wounded.

The fighters' horses are tied in the woods of the ravine. From the rim, the soldiers can see them more easily than the men in the pits. Many of the horses are killed. For people of the buffalo hunt, horses meant food, freedom and speed. It is a heavy loss. Without them, the May-tee will find it much harder to move fast across the prairie.

The battle settles into a deadlock. The soldiers lie along the rim and fire down into the trees. The defenders stay in their pits and fire up. Neither side can move the other. Through the afternoon, many defenders slip away. Doo-mon keeps firing at every target he can find, to give the others heart. Doo-mon later said that Napoléon Nault, Ree-el's cousin, stayed beside him. By some counts, only about fifty are left in the koo-lee. To keep up their courage, Isidore Doo-mon starts an old song about Napoleon, and all the men in the pits join in the chorus.

Doo-mon is down to a few cartridges; he later said he had only seven. He sets the dry grass alight, so that the wind carries fire and smoke toward the soldiers. Under the smoke, the defenders push toward the soldiers' right. Army teamsters run forward and beat out the flames. Along the line, a young bugler of the 90th, William Buchanan, carries ammunition to the men, calling in his high voice: "Now, boys, who's for more cartridges?"

Across the river, the second column hears the firing. Its only scow, a flat river boat, had been sent off that morning to fetch fodder. Soldiers on the far bank shout across the water. Mel-gund cannot make out the words, but guesses that he is needed. When the scow is back, the crossing begins. It holds barely sixty men. With no cable to pull on, the men row it with oars hacked out with axes, against the current, through mud, boulders and blocks of ice, between banks a hundred feet high. About two hundred and fifty men and two guns of the Winnipeg Battery get across without an accident. The Royal Grenadiers, under Captain Mason, come up into the line and take the place of the tired 90th. No source gives the time.

The rain turns to sleet. By about three in the afternoon, Middleton wrote, the firing had almost stopped. Some soldiers ask to rush the last rifle pits. Middleton refuses. He wrote that he could not help "a feeling of admiration and respect for their stubborn defense when deserted by their comrades." On the rim, the soldiers are soaked and cold. In the koo-lee, the few defenders who are left are nearly out of cartridges.

Late in the day, help arrives from Ba-tosh: about seventy horsemen, eighty in Doo-mon's telling, led, by most accounts, by Gabriel's brother, Ay-dwar Doo-mon. Many of the defenders have already gone. This time the May-tee did not wait in a koo-lee on the trail. They dug in around their village. That battle has its own page. The Too-ron family lost their home. The family's own memory, told apart from the shelling, is of soldiers burning it, killing their livestock and taking their belongings; they managed to hide the family clock, which survives today. Less than three weeks later they lost two sons, Calixte and Elzéar, who were killed at Ba-tosh on the 12th of May. Zho-zett Too-ron lived until 1928. The battlefield was named a National Historic Site in 1923. Today it is called the Battle of Too-ron's Koo-lee / Fish Creek National Historic Site, to honour its May-tee name. Archaeologists have found what is probably the cellar of the Too-ron house, and the old trail. Middleton's camp, with a gravestone for some of the soldiers, is a separate site nearby. In Winnipeg, the Volunteer Monument remembers the 90th's dead. The May-tee remember Too-ron's Koo-lee in their own stories, and in Gabriel Doo-mon's account of the battle, which he dictated in 1889.

The day after the battle, a soldier named Thomas Bull wrote to his father about how many of his comrades had fallen. Four days later, the gunners' commander, Captain Drury, wrote his list of wounded on a piece of birch bark. It is kept today in the Royal Canadian Artillery Museum. The army's dead were six men killed outright and four who died of their wounds, among them two gunners of "A" Battery and Lieutenant Charles Swinford of the 90th. With no steamer yet on the river, the army's wounded were carried in makeshift ambulances about forty-two miles to Saskatoon, where settlers nursed them in their homes. One of them, Trooper D'Arcy Baker of Boulton's Scouts, died two days after the battle and was buried beside his comrades. Middleton wrote that his men "had borne their baptism of fire well". The band of the 90th carried in the wounded under fire. Middleton stayed at Fish Creek for about two weeks. He buried his dead, drilled his men, and waited for supplies and the river steamer Northcote, which arrived on the 5th of May. From then on, his army always marched together. Parks Canada calls Fish Creek a May-tee psychological victory: a small force had stopped an army and lost fewer men. Hildebrandt ranks it, with Duck Lake, among the May-tee' greatest military successes. Military historians answer that Middleton soon took back the lead, and Hildebrandt defends his slow, careful advance as the right way to fight an enemy in the bush. Ree-el called it a victory. In a letter to the Cree chief Poundmaker, he wrote that the volunteers at Fish Creek had fought "not only as brave men, but as heroes", and asked for two or three hundred men to come to Ba-tosh. Maxime Lépine, who fought at Fish Creek, remembered it differently: "We prayed all the day, and I think prayer did more than the bullets." The victory had a cost. Many horses were lost, and much of the ammunition was spent. Ree-el allowed no more ambushes. Doo-mon said later that the soldiers could easily have been attacked on the way, "and Ree-el never consented to let them do it." Middleton had learned something too. Before Ba-tosh he said that the May-tee were only dangerous "when you play their game, bush fighting." On the 7th of May the army marched on toward Ba-tosh. Two days later the battle there began. This time the May-tee did not wait in a koo-lee on the trail. They dug in around their village. That battle has its own page. The Too-ron family lost their home. The family's own memory, told apart from the shelling, is of soldiers burning it, killing their livestock and taking their belongings; they managed to hide the family clock, which survives today. Less than three weeks later they lost two sons, Calixte and Elzéar, who were killed at Ba-tosh on the 12th of May. Zho-zett Too-ron lived until 1928. The battlefield was named a National Historic Site in 1923. Today it is called the Battle of Too-ron's Koo-lee / Fish Creek National Historic Site, to honour its May-tee name. Archaeologists have found what is probably the cellar of the Too-ron house, and the old trail. Middleton's camp, with a gravestone for some of the soldiers, is a separate site nearby. In Winnipeg, the Volunteer Monument remembers the 90th's dead. The May-tee remember Too-ron's Koo-lee in their own stories, and in Gabriel Doo-mon's account of the battle, which he dictated in 1889.
